podcast.title: Elvis Presley Inspiration (1955)
podcast.body: Following his discharge from the naval hospital in September 1955, Gene Vincent attended a country music show headlined by Hank Snow, which also featured the Louvin Brothers. However, it was witnessing a young Elvis Presley perform lower down the bill that profoundly changed Vincent's life, inspiring him to pursue a career in rock and roll. "The story seems to be the same for almost every one of the early rockabilly artists... he immediately decides that he wants to do that, that Elvis is doing something that's like what the young man has already started doing, but he's proved that you can do it on stage for people."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Sailor Career and Motorcycle Accident (1955)
podcast.body: Gene Vincent, born Vincent Eugene Craddock, had been content with his career as a sailor until 1955. After reenlisting and receiving a $900 bonus, he purchased a Triumph racing motorbike. This bike was involved in an accident that severely damaged his left leg. The official story attributed the crash to a woman driving a Chrysler, while another account suggested Vincent crashed trying to ride under a naval base security barrier while intoxicated. The accident left his leg shattered, causing chronic osteomyelitis, a permanent open sore, and frequent bone fractures, leading to lifelong pain. He adamantly refused amputation, opting for over a year in a cast followed by a metal brace. "Whatever the truth, his left leg was smashed up, and looked for a long time like it was going to be amputated, but he refused to allow this."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: End of First Wave Rockabilly Success (1956)
podcast.body: By December 1956, Gene Vincent had stopped having hit records, marking the end of the first wave of rockabilly stars, with only Elvis Presley remaining as a dominant white rock and roll figure. "Karl Perkins, Gene Vincent and Bill Haley had stopped having hits, and Johnny Cash had started to be promoted as a country singer, rather than a rock and roller."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Las Vegas Residency Incident (1956)
podcast.body: Gene Vincent and The Blue Caps secured a lucrative Las Vegas residency, earning $3,000 a week, a "staggering sum" for 1956. However, when manager Tex Davis relayed the casino owner's demand (backed by the mafia) for Vincent to tone down his act, Vincent reacted defiantly. He went on stage, performed only one song, then spotted Davis in the crowd, gave him "the finger," and walked off, leaving his band to finish the show without him. This act of insubordination led to the residency's abrupt cancellation and Davis terminating his management contract. "Instead, Jean went on stage, sang one song, found Tex Davis in the crowd, caught his eye, flipped him off, and walked off stage, leaving the band to do the rest of the show without him."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Name Creation (1956)
podcast.body: Born Vincent Eugene Craddock, his stage name, "Gene Vincent," was coined by Capitol Records' Ken Nelson. Nelson ingeniously created the concise stage name by combining elements from Vincent's four given names. "A name Nelson created from Jean's four names."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Darker Image in 1957
podcast.body: In 1957, Gene Vincent was noted for presenting a "darker sound" and a tough, greasy image, often seen in his leather jacket, reflecting a rebellious aesthetic of the time. "In 1957, there was the darker sound of Jean Vincent's looking all tough and greasy in his leather jacket."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Visa Issues on Australian Tour (1957)
podcast.body: Gene Vincent and his band, the Blue Caps, encountered visa problems in Honolulu, causing them to be held up and miss the initial performances of Little Richard's Australian tour in October 1957. "Vincent actually had to miss the first couple of shows, on the tour, as he and the blue cap got held up in Honolulu, apparently due to visa issues, and couldn't continue on to Australia with the rest of the tour until that was sorted out."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Work Permit Restrictions on UK Tour (1962)
podcast.body: On the October 1962 UK tour with Little Richard, Gene Vincent was permitted entry into the country but was not allowed to perform on stage due to work permit issues, so he served as the compere for the early shows and later sang from off stage. "This time Vincent was allowed in the country but wasn't allowed to perform on stage, so he appeared only as the compare, at least at the start of the tour."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Elvis Presley Comparison and Encounter
podcast.body: Many contemporaries commented on the sonic and stylistic similarities between Gene Vincent's "Be-Bop-A-Lula" and Elvis Presley's music. Anecdotes circulated, including Elvis's mother mistakenly liking "Be-Bop-A-Lula" as if it were her son's, and Elvis himself allegedly being confused. Despite these resemblances, Vincent's voice was described as thinner, tenser, and twitchier compared to Elvis's consistently playful, exuberant, and controlled delivery at the time. When Vincent eventually met Elvis, he offered an apology for any perceived copying, but Elvis reassured him that he understood and that it was simply "just how Gene sang." "While Elvis is fully in control at all times, playful and exuberant, Gene Vincent is tense and twitchy."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: Erratic Behavior and Career Decline
podcast.body: Already known for being impetuous before his accident, Gene Vincent's chronic pain from his leg injury, combined with the pressures of rock and roll stardom and heavy drinking, exacerbated his erratic behavior. This included breaking contracts, his outburst in Las Vegas, and pulling a gun on band members on multiple occasions. This increasingly unstable conduct, coupled with Capitol Records' and Ken Nelson's misunderstanding of rock and roll, ultimately led to Vincent becoming a "forgotten figure" in the United States. "Vincent's increasingly erratic behaviour including pulling a gun on band members on multiple occasions, and Capital and Ken Nelson's lack of understanding of rock and roll music meant that he quickly became a forgotten figure in the US."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Inspiration for Songwriting
podcast.body: During a tour with Gene Vincent (and Eddie Cochrane), Roy Orbison noted that many artists on the bill had only a single hit and lacked a steady source of new material. This observation motivated Orbison to commit to songwriting as his principal art. "He realised that they, and the other people on the bill, had one hit each. Cochrane would later have more, but still, Orbison wondered where those people's other hits were going to come from, where were they going to find their material."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Post-Rockabilly Chart Performance
podcast.body: Gene Vincent was one of the few exceptions among Elvis's peers who didn't transition to orchestrated pop or pure country, but he was "no longer having hits, at least in the US" after rockabilly faded. "with the exception of a handful like Jean Vincent, who were no longer having hits, at least in the US."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Recorded First Records at Owen Bradley's Studio
podcast.body: Gene Vincent made his first records at Owen Bradley's studio in Nashville, the same studio where the Rock and Roll Trio later recorded. "the same one where Gene Vincent made his first records."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Rockabilly Fizzle
podcast.body: Gene Vincent was among the white rockabilly acts that experienced a surge in popularity throughout 1955 and 1956 but saw their US chart success "fizzle" by late 1956, preventing them from having another major domestic hit. Despite this, he achieved success in other countries and continued to create significant music in the years that followed. "While Perkins, Gene Vincent and Bill Haley would between them never have another major hit in the US, though all of them would have success in other countries and make important music over the next few years."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Successful Crossover Artist
podcast.body: Gene Vincent is cited as a rockabilly artist whose music achieved crossover success, differentiating his career path from Wanda Jackson, whose "I Gotta Know" did not cross over. His producer, Ken Nelson, also made mistakes with his material, similar to Jackson's experience.

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: UK Image Reinvention (1950s)
podcast.body: Gene Vincent had a profound impact in the United Kingdom, largely thanks to TV producer Jack Good, who was instrumental in introducing rock and roll to British television. Good suggested Vincent abandon his conventional stage wear in favor of black leather and encouraged him to accentuate the postural problems caused by his disability. Vincent's appearances on shows like "Boy Meets Girls," dressed in black leather, hunched over and seemingly in pain, defined the visual archetype of a rock and roll star for British teenagers of the 1950s, particularly at a time when few American rock and roll acts visited or received TV exposure in the UK. "Vincent's appearances on Boy Meets Girls, dressed in black leather, hunched over, in pain because of his leg, defined for British teenagers of the 1950s what a rock and roll it was meant to look like."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

xref.title: Toronto Rock and Roll Revival Performance (September 13, 1969)
xref.body: John Lennon performed at Varsity Stadium in Toronto, facing severe stage fright and heroin withdrawal, as it was his first performance outside The Beatles. He was also intimidated by other acts on the bill, including his idols Chuck Berry, Gene Vincent, and Little Richard. "This was the first time John had ever performed outside the Beatles, which at the time were still a going concern."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
